It also requires you to understand how these two concepts interact with each other. A is wrong because it suggests that the federal court can exercise jurisdiction over a case arising under state law simply because Congress has authorized them to do so. But this would violate the constitutional limitation on federal judicial power set forth in Article III, Section 2. B is wrong as well; it assumes that the court may grant summary judgment based upon its conclusion that the claim fails to arise under federal law. However, the court should have dismissed the case instead, since it lacked jurisdiction from the beginning. Section 1257 gives the Court the power to review any state court judgment that decides whether a state statute conflicts with federal law, or that interprets a federal statute. So B is wrong. The Court can review the state court’s ruling interpreting the federal statute, just as it can review rulings striking down state statutes as unconstitutional. C is also wrong. Section 1257 is clearly within the bounds of the Court’s Article III jurisdiction, since it authorizes review of cases that raise federal issues. The fact that those issues arise in a case based on state law does not matter. As we saw earlier, the Court has the power to review such cases under Osborn. E is obviously silly. Now let us turn to the real choice here. D suggests that the Court can review both of the state court’s rulings. That seems plausible enough. After all, the first ruling involved a federal issue—the constitutionality of the federal statute—and the second involved the proper interpretation of a federal statute. Both seem to fall squarely within the terms of §1257(a). But wait! What about A? Doesn’t it suggest something very similar? Yes, it does. But there is a crucial difference between them. D says that the Court can review both rulings, while A says that it cannot review either. Why the discrepancy? Because A focuses on the basis of the suit below, rather than on the nature of the issues decided by the state court. The Mottleys filed suit against the airline under state contract law. They didn’t sue under the federal statute, so their case ‘‘doesn’t arise under’’ federal law. Therefore, according to A, the Supreme Court lacks the power to review the state court’s decision in the case. But that conclusion ignores the fact that the state court made two rulings in the case, each of which falls within the scope of §1257. The first ruled that the federal statute was unconstitutional, and the second construed the federal statute. Each of these rulings presents a federal issue, and thus comes within the scope of §1267. The fact that the underlying action was based on state law does not prevent the Court from reviewing the state court’s resolution of the federal issues presented during the litigation. Indeed, the Court often reviews state court decisions that resolve federal issues in actions based on state law. For example, the Court frequently hears appeals from state criminal convictions, in which the defendant challenges his conviction on grounds that he was denied rights guaranteed him by the Fourteenth Amendment. These cases don’t arise under federal law, yet the Court regularly exercises appellate jurisdiction over them. See generally 28 U.S.C.§1257(3); see also Michigan v. Long, 463 U.S. 1032 (1983)(holding that the Supreme Court has the power to review state court decisions rejecting Fourth Amendment claims, even though the case arises under state law). So A is wrong too. The Court can review the state supreme court’s rulings on the federal issues, even though the case arose under state law. D is the best answer. The Court can review both of the state supreme court’s rulINGS, since both present federal issues falling within the scope of §1275. Of course, the Court won’t necessarily take every case that meets the requirements of §1257. It receives thousands of petitions for certiorari each year, and accepts far fewer than ten percent of them. But it certainly has the power to accept the petition in this case, should it choose to do so. Final answer: D

So, even though Ivens didn’t sign on, the case may still be removed. D is wrong, too. What about the thirty-day time limit on raising defects in removal? Doesn’t that bar the motion to remand? Nope. Section 1447(d) allows a motion based on failure to remove within the statutory time frame anytime during the pendency of the action. So, C wins. Final answer: C

But that doesn’t make much sense. Under §1441(c), once you’ve established that the case is removable, all claims in the case will go along for the ride. There is no separate analysis of removability for individual claims. So D is out. C also looks like a loser. It says that the case wasn’t properly removed because Rasmussen should have removed it earlier, based on diversity. But that’s just plain wrong. Once a case has become removable, it stays removable until judgment. See 28 U.S.C.§1446(d); see also Exxon Mobil Corp. v. Allapattah Services Inc., 545 U.S. 540 (2005). So even though the case might have been removable before, it still remains removable now. That leaves us with B and A. Which do we choose? Well, let’s look again at the facts. When Rasmussen filed his complaint, he only had a state-law claim against Apex. Since Apex is from Texas, the same state where suit was brought, the case couldn’t be removed under §1441(b)(1). After the amendment adding the Lanham Act claim, however, the case becomes removable. Now, there is a federal claim, and the diversity claim is gone. So the case meets the requirements of §1441(a): it is a case over which the federal court has original jurisdiction. And since there is no longer an in-state defendant, the bar to removal in §1441(b)(l) does not apply either. So the case is removable. But wait—what about the remaining state-law claim? Doesn’t the presence of that claim prevent removal? Nope. As noted above, §1441(c) allows the entire case to be removed, including non-federal claims, if the case is otherwise removable. Allahpattah Servs., Inc., 545 U.s. 540 (2oo5). So here, too, the case is removable despite the presence of the state-law claim. So B is right, and A is wrong. Final answer: B

So A is wrong; Mary does have sufficient contacts with California to support jurisdiction over her if they relate to the claim. B is also wrong. While it may well be true that defending the case in California would impose great hardship on Mary, the Supreme Court held in Burnham v. Superior Court, 495 U.S. 604 (1990), that a defendant who appears in court cannot complain about being sued where he appeared. In that case, the Court said that the plaintiff could not sue the car dealer in Oklahoma just because the car broke down there, even though the dealer might find it very convenient to defend the case in New York or Pennsylvania. Even though it will be burdensome for Mary to travel from Massachusetts to California to defend herself, she chose to go to California voluntarily, so she must accept the consequences of doing business there. She can’t avoid liability by claiming that it would be too expensive to come back to defend herself!

B is also wrong. This is not a doing-business-in-the-state case. Dispos-All doesn’t sell anything in Maryland, nor does it advertise or solicit sales from customers who live in Maryland. But C is right. Dispos-All should know that waste dumped in Delaware will flow down the river to Maryland. If it dumps toxic chemicals in the river, they’ll end up in Maryland as well. So it should reasonably anticipate being sued in Maryland over injuries caused by its dumping practices. D is wrong too. They got there by flowing downstream, which was certainly not what Dispos-All intended. And while Dispos-All could foresee that its actions might injure people in Maryland (and elsewhere), it did not deliberately reach out to those states. Its conduct was directed toward Delaware only. This question tests your understanding of the effect of Shaffer v. Heitner on the availability of quasi in rem jurisdiction. A is clearly an attempt to assert quasi in rem type I jurisdiction. Ohora seeks to recover damages for an injury suffered on Roux’s land in Nebraska. Her suit arises directly out of events occurring on the land, and she seeks to enforce her rights in the land through the litigation. Thus, if she can establish jurisdiction over Roux himself, she may sue him here for the tort committed on the land. B involves a suit to determine title to real estate located within the forum state. Again, if the court has jurisdiction over Roux, it will have power to decide the dispute about title to the land. C is more difficult. It appears to involve quasi in rem type II jurisdiction. Consolidated does not seek to enforce its rights in the crane; rather, it seeks to recover on an unrelated claim arising elsewhere, using the presence of the crane in Nebraska as a basis for jurisdiction. However, the Court’s statement in Shaffer that all exercises of jurisdiction should now be judged by the minimum contacts test suggests that even this case might fail. After all, the crane is just another asset of Roux, like the stock in Shaffer. Why shouldn’t the rule announced in Shaffer apply equally to both? Indeed, some courts have taken this position. See, e.g., World-Wide Volkswagen Corp. v. Woodson, 444 U.S. 286, 297 n.18 (1980); see generally Wright & Miller, Federal Practice and Procedure §§1067–1068 (1973 Supp.). But others have rejected this view, arguing that Shaffer left intact the authority to assert quasi in rem type II jurisdiction where the property attached is related to the transaction giving rise to the claim. See, e.g., United States v. First Nat’l Bank of St. Paul, 376 F.2d 224 (8th Cir.), cert. denied sub nom. McGowan v. United States, 389 U.S. 821 (1967); see generally Wright & Miller, supra, §1068. Under this approach, C would still be valid after Shaffer. D is wrong, since C is probably still good law after Shaffer. E is wrong too, since A is certainly still good law after Shaffer. Final answer: A

[/THINK]

[THINK]
The first option suggests that all exercises of in rem jurisdiction are unconstitutional after Shaffer. That can’t be true; the Court has never suggested that. Indeed, in Shaffer itself, the Court noted that the case before it didn’t involve a situation where the parties were disputing title to the res, but rather a dispute about management of the corporation whose stock was being sequestered. See id. at 207 n.10. Thus, the Court left open the possibility that some uses of in rem jurisdiction might still survive. Option B suggests that both forms of quasi in rem jurisdiction have been eliminated by Shaffer. Again, however, the Court made clear that it wasn’t eliminating all quasi in rem jurisdiction, just the kind of jurisdiction exercised in Shaffer, which was type II. Id. at 207–08 & nn.10–11. Type I quasi in rem jurisdiction remains viable today. Consider, for example, a suit brought by a creditor seeking to foreclose her mortgage lien on real estate located within the forum state. She may sue the debtor in personam if she can establish minimum contacts, but even if she cannot, she will likely prevail on her action to enforce the lien. The reason is simple: The debtor owns land in the forum state, and the creditor seeks to recover possession of that land. Under the analysis in Shaffer, this is a valid exercise of quasi in rem jurisdiction, since the creditor is suing to recover the very thing that gives rise to the court’s power—the mortgaged land. Similarly, a party may bring a suit to quiet title to land located in the forum state, even though the defendant does not reside there. These suits do not violate due process, because they seek recovery of the very thing that supports the court’s jurisdiction. They are thus analogous to the classic in rem actions discussed earlier. So C is wrong too. D is the best choice here. While Shaffer rejected the use of quasi in rem type II jurisdiction, it did not reject either in rem or quasi in rem type I jurisdiction. Both remain available today.

Final answer: D
[/THINK]

This question tests your understanding of the relationship between the constitutional limits on personal jurisdiction and the statutory authorization for it. It asks what standard the federal judge should use in deciding whether to assert personal jurisdiction over Jason. D suggests that the judge should look at the Fifth Amendment, which governs the federal court’s authority to exercise jurisdiction. B suggests that the judge should consider both the Fifth Amendment and the Arizona long-arm statute. C suggests that the judge should focus solely on the Fourteenth Amendment, while E suggests that the judge needn’t worry about personal jurisdiction issues at all, once the case is removed to federal court. A suggests that the judge should decide whether the Arizona courts could constitutionally exercise jurisdiction over Jason. Which test is right? Well, we know that the federal court cannot exercise jurisdiction beyond the bounds set by the Constitution. So, even though the Arizona longarm statute might authorize jurisdiction over Jason, the federal court couldn’t exercise it if doing so would violate the Fifth Amendment. And, although the Fifth Amendment allows more expansive jurisdiction than the Fourteenth, the federal court still needs statutory authorization before it exercises jurisdiction. If there were no statute allowing the federal court to exercise jurisdiction over Jason, it wouldn’t matter how strong his contacts with the United States were—he’d get off scot-free! So, the federal court must find that it is authorized to exercise jurisdiction over him. That means that it must determine whether the Arizona long-arm statute authorizes it to do so. After all, Rule 4(k)(1)(a) says that the federal court can exercise jurisdiction over a defendant if the state courts could. So, the federal court must ask itself whether the Arizona courts could exercise jurisdiction over Jason. To make that determination, the federal court looks first to the Arizona long-arm statute. If it doesn’t authorize jurisdiction, then neither will the federal court. If it does authorize jurisdiction, the federal court must next determine whether asserting jurisdiction over Jason would satisfy the requirements of the Fourteenth Amendment. If it would, the federal court can exercise jurisdiction over him. If it wouldn’t, the federal court can’t either. So, the proper inquiry here is whether the Arizona long-arm statute authoriz es jurisdiction over Jason, and whether it would be consistent with the Fourteenth Amendment to exercise it. Therefore, A is best. B is wrong because it focuses on the Fifth Amendment instead of the Fourteenth. While the Fifth Amendment sets outer boundaries on the federal court’s ability to exercise jurisdiction, the federal court must also comply with the Fourteenth Amendment when determining whether to exercise jurisdiction over a defendant. Otherwise, the federal court could exercise jurisdiction over a defendant whose contacts with the forum state did not justify it, just because they supported jurisdiction somewhere else in the country. For example, suppose that Jason had never entered Arizona, but had sold goods to a customer in New York. He would certainly be subject to jurisdiction in New York, under the Fourteenth Amendment. But he shouldn’t be forced to litigate in Arizona, simply because he was willing to sell products into the stream of commerce. The Fourteenth Amendment requires that he have sufficient contacts with Arizona to justify requiring him to defend there. So, the federal court must examine the Arizona long-arm statute and the Fourteenth Amendment to determine whether it can properly exercise jurisdiction over Jason. C is wrong because it ignores the role played by the Arizona long-arm statute. The federal court can’t exercise jurisdiction over Jason merely because it would be constitutional to do so. It must also be authorized by statute. Since the federal court’s jurisdiction derives from the Arizona long-arm statute, it must follow the terms of that statute. If the statute doesn’t authorize jurisdiction, the federal court can’t exercise it, regardless of the strength of Jason’s contacts with Arizona. D is wrong because it fails to take account of the fact that the federal court’s jurisdiction depends upon the Arizona long-arm statute. The Fifth Amendment gives the federal court the power to exercise jurisdiction over anyone who has contacts with the United States, but the federal court isn’t free to exercise jurisdiction whenever those contacts exist. It must act pursuant to congressional authorization, usually found in the rules. Here, the rules say that the federal court can exercise jurisdiction only if the Arizona courts could. So, the federal judge must look to the Arizona long-arm statute and theFourteenth Amendment to determine whether the Arizona courts could exercise jurisdiction. E is wrong because removal to federal court does not waive objections to personal jurisdiction. Indeed, the federal court must address the issue of personal jurisdiction sua sponte, even if the parties don’t raise it. See Fed. R. Civ. P 12(h)(3).

Final answer: A
[/THINK]

[THINK]
This question presents two issues. First, whether the New York long-arm statute supports jurisdiction here; second, whether it would be constitutional to exercise jurisdiction even if the statute supported it. Let’s start by looking at the first issue—whether the long-arm statute applies. Under the ‘‘transacting business’’ prong of the New York long-arm statute, the court may assert jurisdiction where the defendant ‘‘engages in any business transactions within the state . . . and such contacts shall also give the courts of this state jurisdiction to enter judgment against such person on causes of action arising from or related thereto.’’ N.Y.C.P.L.R. §302(a)(1). This seems pretty clear. Ausable engaged in a business transaction (the sale) in New York, and the cause of action arises out of that transaction. So, the long-arm statute should apply. Right? Well, maybe not quite so fast. There’s a catch. The New York Court of Appeals has held that the ‘‘business transactions’’ clause only reaches defendants who engage in repeated transactions in the state. See, e.g., Landoil Resources Corp. v. Alexander & Assocs., Inc., 776 N.E.2d 58, 69–70 (N.Y. 2002); see also McGowan v. Smith, 52 N.Y.S.2d 641, 643 (App. Div. 1st Dep’t 1944), aff’d mem., 298 N.Y. 657, 83 N.E.2d 176 (1948). Thus, the fact that Ausable made a single sale in New York probably won’t suffice to bring it into court there. So B looks better now. But wait! What about C? Even though the long-arm statute doesn’t cover this situation, could the court still exercise jurisdiction based upon the Due Process Clause? After all, the Supreme Court has said that a single contact with the forum state can sometimes justify exercising jurisdiction. For example, in World-Wide Volkswagen Corp. v. Woodson, 444 U.S. 286 (1980), the Court upheld jurisdiction over a car dealer sued in Oklahoma after selling a car to a customer in Texas, who then drove through Oklahoma en route home. And in Burger King Corp. v. Rudzewicz, 471 U.S. 462 (1985), the Court found that a Florida restaurant franchisee was subject to suit in Florida, despite having no physical presence there, because he had entered into a contract with the franchisor in Florida. So, couldn’t the court find that it would be constitutional to exercise personal jurisdiction over Ausable, even though she didn’t make enough sales in New York to trigger the long-arm statute? Maybe, but I doubt it. While the Supreme Court has recognized that a single contact can sometimes support jurisdiction, it has never suggested that a single isolated contact would ever be sufficient. Rather, the Court has emphasized that the defendant’s activities must create a relationship between her and the forum state that makes it reasonable to require her to defend herself there. See, e.g., Asahi Metal Indus. Co. v. Superior Ct., 480 U.S. 102, 112 (1987) (‘‘The due process analysis requires us to evaluate both the burden imposed on the nonresident defendant and the interests served by requiring him to litigate in the forum State.’’) A single sale in New York hardly creates such a connection. Indeed, the Supreme Court has specifically rejected the argument that a single sale in the forum state suffices to establish minimum contacts. See Helgeland v. Puritan Marine Ins. Underwriters Corp., 466 F. Supp. 1226, 1230 n.1 (D.Del. 1979) (citing cases holding that a single sale in the forum does not constitute doing business there for purposes of general jurisdiction, and noting that ‘‘it appears that the same rule applies to specific jurisdiction as well’’). So, while the long-arm statute doesn’t reach this case, neither does the Due Process Clause. Therefore, the case will almost certainly be dismissed. Final answer: B

[/THINK]

Rule 4(d)(1) requires him to enclose both the summons and the complaint with the request for waiver. If he doesn’t, the waiver won’t take effect even if the defendant signs it. See Fed. R. Civ. The best choice here is C. It satisfies all requirements for service of process under Rule 4(e) (service within a judicial district of the United States), since Indiana is part of the Seventh Circuit. And it establishes personal jurisdiction over both defendants because they have sufficient contacts with Indiana. Donitz has lived there most of his life, and Preferred’s president resides there as well. See International Shoe Co. v. Washington, 326 U.S. 310 (1945). A also fails, because while the Ohio service-of-process rule would authorize this method of serving Preferred, it doesn’t provide authority to serve Donitz individually. E is clearly wrong—they could sue in Indiana! So C wins.

This is a good example of how important it is to read the statutes carefully. D suggests that §1406(a) does not allow transfer here because the Eastern District of Kentucky isn’t a proper venue. That’s true; the statute says that the court shall either dismiss or transfer the case ‘to any district . . . in which it could have been brought,’ i.e., a proper venue. So, the court cannot transfer to the Eastern District of Kentucky. But C argues that the court must transfer to the Western District of Kentucky, since it is a proper venue. Not quite right. While the statute authorizes transfer to a proper venue, it doesn’t require it. Rather, it leaves the decision whether to dismiss or transfer up to the discretion of the trial judge. B gets it just right. The court may choose between dismissal and transfer to a proper venue. A is off base. Even though the court hasn’t been asked to transfer the case, it still has the power to do so under §1406(a); indeed, the statute expressly grants the court the option of transfer without requiring a request from the parties. E is wrong too. Transfer under §1404(a) requires that the case be pending in a proper venue. Since it wasn’t, §1404(a) won’t help here.

Final answer: B
[/THINK]

This is a toughie! Let’s start with A. It suggests that venue is proper here based on Section 1391(b)(3), which provides that venue will lie where ‘‘any defendant resides if all defendants reside within the same state.’’ But wait—this provision doesn’t say anything about personal jurisdiction. So how can we use it? We need some other basis for finding that the defendants ‘‘reside’’ in the forum state before we can invoke (b)(3). In fact, the Supreme Court has held that the term ‘‘resides,’’ as used in the venue statutes, means ‘‘domiciled.’’ See Neirbo Co. v.
